title: Converting a public company into a private company
law: Sections 13 and 14, Companies Act, 2013; Rule 41, Companies (Incorporation) Rules, 2014
summary: Changes a public company into a private company by special resolution, advertisement to creditors and approval of the Regional Director.
when: When a public company wants to become a private company, for example to drop public-company restrictions.
applies: Unlisted public companies; the company must keep members to 200 or fewer after conversion

steps.d: Give notice to all directors. At the meeting, approve the conversion, the changes to the MOA and AOA, the EGM date, time and place, and the draft EGM notice with explanatory statement.
steps.time: At least 7 days' notice, or shorter notice as the law allows
docs: Draft EGM notice with explanatory statement

steps.d: Pass a special resolution to convert the company, alter the MOA and AOA, and authorise the filing of forms and documents.
steps.time: At least 21 clear days' notice, or shorter notice with consent of the required majority of members

steps.d: File the certified board resolution, the EGM notice with explanatory statement, the certified special resolution and the altered MOA and AOA.
Publish the notice once in an English newspaper and once in a vernacular newspaper circulating in the district of the registered office. Do this after MGT-14 and before RD-1.
Send notice to every creditor and debenture holder, and to the Registrar and Regional Director and other regulators concerned. Keep postal receipts and acknowledgements as proof.
steps.time: Give 21 clear days before filing RD-1, counted from the advertisement
docs: Notices to creditors and debenture holders

steps.t: Prepare the creditor list and declarations
steps.d: Prepare the list of creditors and debenture holders, made up to a date within 30 days before filing, showing nature, amount and age of each dues. Get the director's affidavit and declarations.

steps.t: File RD-1 with the Regional Director
steps.d: File the application with all attachments. The Registrar sends the Regional Director a report on the application. Keep a gap of at least 21 days between the advertisement and RD-1.
docs: EGM minutes showing votes for, against and neutral
Power of attorney or memorandum of appearance

steps.d: After the Regional Director's order, file the order with the Registrar.
File the conversion form with the order attached, to give effect to the change of status.

forms.purpose: Filing of special resolution and board resolution
Covering form for the application, as named in the reference note
Notice of the Regional Director's order

checklist: Members after conversion will not exceed 200 (not counting present and past employees)
No deposits taken in breach of sections 73 to 76A
No pending resolution to be filed under section 179(3)
Financial statements and annual returns are up to date
List of creditors and debenture holders ready
Proof of postal delivery to creditors kept

meetings.title: Board meeting to approve the conversion
meetings.notice_days: At least 7 days (shorter if allowed by law)

meetings.title: Extraordinary general meeting for conversion
meetings.notice_days: At least 21 clear days (shorter with consent)

resolutions.title: Approval of conversion to a private company
resolutions.text: RESOLVED THAT, subject to the approval of the members and the Regional Director, the company be converted from a public company into a private company under Sections 13 and 14 of the Companies Act, 2013 and Rule 41 of the Companies (Incorporation) Rules, 2014. RESOLVED FURTHER THAT the draft altered Memorandum and Articles of Association placed before the meeting be approved for submission to the members. RESOLVED FURTHER THAT [name of director], Director, be authorised to take all steps needed to give effect to this resolution.

resolutions.title: Fixing the EGM and approving the notice
resolutions.text: RESOLVED THAT an Extraordinary General Meeting of {co} be held on [date] at [time] at [place] to consider the conversion. RESOLVED FURTHER THAT the draft notice with the explanatory statement under Section 102 be approved and [name of director / company secretary] be authorised to issue it to every member and every other person entitled to receive it.

resolutions.title: Special resolution for conversion and alteration of MOA and AOA
resolutions.text: RESOLVED THAT, pursuant to Sections 13 and 14 of the Companies Act, 2013 and Rule 41 of the Companies (Incorporation) Rules, 2014, and subject to the approval of the Regional Director, the company be converted from a public company into a private company. RESOLVED FURTHER THAT the Memorandum of Association be altered by deleting the word 'Public' from the company's name and the Articles of Association be replaced by the new Articles placed before the meeting, containing the restrictions required by Section 2(68). RESOLVED FURTHER THAT the new name be '{co} Private Limited'.
resolutions.explanatory: The Board proposes to convert the company into a private company because [reason]. Section 14 requires a special resolution and the approval of the Regional Director. The altered Memorandum and Articles are open for inspection at the registered office on all working days between [time] and [time]. No director or key managerial personnel is interested in this resolution except as a member, to the extent of their shareholding.

resolutions.title: Authority to file forms and documents
resolutions.text: RESOLVED THAT [name of director], Director, and [name of company secretary], Company Secretary, be authorised, singly, to sign and file Forms MGT-14, RD-1, INC-28 and INC-27 and any other forms, applications, affidavits and documents, to publish advertisements and to appear before the Registrar and the Regional Director, for giving effect to the conversion.

docs.title: Newspaper advertisement for conversion (Form INC-25A content)
paras: Before the Regional Director, [region], Ministry of Corporate Affairs. In the matter of {co}, having its registered office at [address].

Notice is given to the public that {co} intends to apply to the Central Government (Regional Director) under Section 14 of the Companies Act, 2013 for approval to convert from a public company into a private company, as approved by a special resolution passed at its Extraordinary General Meeting held on [date].

Any person whose interest is likely to be affected may send written objections, with the nature of the interest and grounds, to the Regional Director at [address], with a copy to the company at its registered office, within 21 days of this notice.
By order of the Board, for {co}. [Name of director], [DIN], [date], [place].

docs.title: Notice to creditors and debenture holders
paras: To [name of creditor / debenture holder], [address].

{co} has passed a special resolution on [date] to convert from a public company into a private company. It intends to apply to the Regional Director, [region], for approval under Section 14 of the Companies Act, 2013.
The list of creditors and debenture holders is available for inspection at the registered office. You may send any objection to the company or the Regional Director within 21 days of this notice.
For {co}, [name of director], [date].

docs.title: Declaration by director under Rule 41
paras: I, [name of director], Director of {co}, declare that: (a) the company limits its members to 200 (not counting present and past employees); (b) the company has not accepted deposits in contravention of sections 73 to 76A; (c) it has complied with sections 177, 178, 185, 186 and 188; and (d) no resolution under Section 179(3) is pending to be filed.
Signed at [place] on [date]. [Name], [DIN].

flags: The reference note says the application is filed in 'Form GNL-1' together with RD-1. Rule 41 asks for a plain paper application attached to RD-1; GNL-1 is only a general attachment form. Confirm on the portal what is needed.
The reference note asks for the board resolution to be filed in MGT-14. Section 117(3) lists only specific board resolutions; check if the conversion approval is one before filing it.
The reference note names INC-25A for the newspaper advertisement. INC-25A is the form used under Rule 41 for the notice and the declarations. Check the current MCA form list.
The reference note lists INC-28 and INC-27 both within 15 days of the order. I believe INC-27 is the primary conversion form and INC-28 is the notice of the order; confirm the sequence on the portal.
Section 14 as amended gives the power to the Central Government, exercised by the Regional Director. Older references to the Tribunal are outdated.
Ensure the new AOA contains the restrictions in Section 2(68) (limit on members, restriction on share transfer, ban on public invitation).

title: Converting a private company into an LLP
law: Section 56 and Fourth Schedule, Limited Liability Partnership Act, 2008; Rules 18 and 39, LLP Rules, 2009
summary: Moves a private company into LLP form with approval of members, name reservation, conversion filing and LLP agreement.
when: When the members of a private company want to run the business as an LLP instead.
applies: Private companies (and, under the LLP Act, unlisted public companies); all members become partners

steps.d: Confirm the company is a private company. The reference note also asks for no outstanding loans, no pending litigation, and at least two directors and two partners (see flags). Plan for at least two partners.
Pass a resolution approving the conversion to an LLP.

steps.t: Issue notice and hold the EGM
steps.d: Send the notice to all members and directors. At the meeting, pass a special resolution approving the conversion and approve the draft LLP agreement.
steps.time: At least 21 days' notice, or shorter with consent of the required majority

steps.d: File the board resolution and special resolution with the Registrar with fees.
Apply on the MCA portal to reserve the proposed LLP name.
After the name is approved, file the application to convert the company to an LLP with attachments.
docs: List of partners and their consents

steps.d: After the Registrar approves the conversion, file the initial LLP agreement.

steps.t: Inform the Registrar of the conversion
steps.d: File the notice of conversion along with the certificate of incorporation of the LLP.
steps.time: Within 15 days of registration of the LLP
docs: Certificate of incorporation of the LLP

steps.d: Open a new bank account and complete registrations with other authorities where needed.

forms.purpose: Filing of board and special resolutions
Reserve unique name for the LLP
Application for conversion to an LLP
Notice of conversion to the Registrar

checklist: At least two partners, including two designated partners
Draft LLP agreement approved by EGM
Statement of assets and liabilities prepared
Proof of registered office of the LLP ready

meetings.title: Board meeting to approve conversion to an LLP
meetings.notice_days: At least 7 days (shorter if allowed by law)

meetings.title: Extraordinary general meeting for the LLP conversion
meetings.notice_days: At least 21 clear days (shorter with consent)

resolutions.title: Board approval of conversion to an LLP
resolutions.text: RESOLVED THAT, subject to the approval of the members, the company be converted into a Limited Liability Partnership under Section 56 and the Fourth Schedule of the Limited Liability Partnership Act, 2008 and Rules 18 and 39 of the LLP Rules, 2009. RESOLVED FURTHER THAT the notice of an Extraordinary General Meeting to be held on [date] at [time] at [place], with the draft LLP agreement, be approved. RESOLVED FURTHER THAT [name of director] be authorised to apply for the LLP name and file all forms.

resolutions.title: Special resolution for conversion and LLP agreement
resolutions.text: RESOLVED THAT, pursuant to Section 56 and the Fourth Schedule of the Limited Liability Partnership Act, 2008, the company be converted into a Limited Liability Partnership named [proposed name of LLP], with [names of partners] as partners and [names] as designated partners. RESOLVED FURTHER THAT the draft LLP agreement placed before the meeting be approved. RESOLVED FURTHER THAT [name of director] be authorised to sign and file Forms RUN-LLP, FiLLiP (Form 18), Form 3, Form 14 and MGT-14 and any other documents.
resolutions.explanatory: The Board proposes to convert the company into an LLP for [reason]. All members will become partners in the LLP on the terms in the draft LLP agreement, open for inspection at the registered office. No director is interested except as a member.

flags: The reference note says the company must have no outstanding loans and no pending litigation. The LLP Act (Fourth Schedule) does not impose these; it needs the consent of secured creditors and requires that all members become partners. Verify before relying.

The reference note says the company needs two directors and two partners. The LLP law needs at least two partners including two designated partners (one resident in India); there is no director count rule for the LLP.

The LLP Act itself does not need a special resolution of the company; it needs consent of all members. The reference note follows Companies Act style; the special resolution and MGT-14 are kept here as the reference note says, but check whether MGT-14 is needed.
Form numbers 14 and 18 and the timelines for Form 3 and Form 14 should be checked against the current LLP forms on the MCA portal.
The reference note lists no timeline for the Registrar's approval. The company ceases to exist and its registration is removed on conversion; confirm current practice.

title: Registering the creation or change of a charge
law: Sections 77 to 81 and 85, Companies Act, 2013; Companies (Registration of Charges) Rules, 2014
summary: Covers registering a new charge or a change to one with the Registrar, late filing rules and the company's register of charges.
when: When a company creates a charge on its assets (for example for a loan) or changes the terms of an existing one.
applies: All companies; private companies get no exemption

steps.d: Authorise a director or KMP to sign documents, submit them to authorities and file e-forms with the Registrar.
steps.time: Before the charge documents are signed

steps.t: File the form with the Registrar
steps.d: Use CHG-1 for general charges and CHG-9 for charges securing debentures.
steps.time: Within 30 days of creation or change

steps.d: If the 30 days are missed, file within the next 30 days with additional fee: 3 times the normal fee for small companies and OPCs, 6 times for others.

If 60 days are missed, file within a further 60 days. Pay normal fee, additional fee and an ad valorem fee: 0.025% of the charge (maximum Rs.1 lakh) for small companies and OPCs; 0.05% (maximum Rs.5 lakh) for others.

If the company does not register in time, the charge-holder may apply. The Registrar notifies the company; if it does not respond within 14 days, the Registrar may register on payment of the prescribed fees.

Give date and nature of instrument, charge ID if modifying, location, type of charge, charge-holder details (name, address, email, PAN), amount secured, property description, main terms, property ownership, earlier charge and present modification.

Give purpose, charge ID, type of debentures, who is applying, instrument date, charge type, property address, trustee or holder details, debenture series (issue date, maximum amount, registration, MGT-14), terms, commission or discount, and modification details.

Attach instruments of creation or modification. Board resolution and sanction letter are optional. For CHG-9, attach the resolution authorising the debenture issue (mandatory) and any Central Government order if filed for rectification.

The form is signed by a director, manager, company secretary, CEO, CFO, IRP, RP, liquidator or authorised representative of a foreign company, and by the charge-holder. It is certified by a practising CA, CS or CMA where required.
On payment of fees the Registrar issues CHG-2 (creation) or CHG-3 (modification).
Maintain the register in Form CHG-7 at the registered office, in physical or electronic form.

forms.deadline: Within 30 days of creation or modification
Within 30 days of creation or modification

forms.purpose: Certificate of registration of charge (issued by Registrar)
Certificate of modification of charge (issued by Registrar)
Register of charges kept by the company

checklist: Board resolution authorising the signatory passed
Charge-holder's name, address, email and PAN
Description and ownership of the property charged
Amount secured and key terms noted
Charge ID noted for any modification
Digital signatures of company and charge-holder ready

meetings.title: Board meeting to authorise the charge filing
meetings.notice_days: At least 7 days (shorter if allowed by law)

resolutions.title: Authority to create or modify a charge and file forms
resolutions.text: RESOLVED THAT the company create a charge / modify the existing charge (Charge ID [charge id]) on [description of property] in favour of [name of charge-holder] to secure [description and amount of facility in Rs.], on the terms placed before the meeting, under Sections 77 to 81 of the Companies Act, 2013. RESOLVED FURTHER THAT [name of director / KMP] be authorised to sign the instruments, submit them to the concerned authorities and file Form CHG-1 / CHG-9 with the Registrar within the time allowed by law.

flags: The reference note lists late fees as 3 times and 6 times followed by a second 60-day window. The 2022 amendment to the Registration of Charges Rules uses different multiples and stages; check the current Rule 12 table.
Section headings given for 79 to 81 look doubtful (I believe 80 deals with modification of charge and 81 with Tribunal relief). Check the Act text.
The reference note omits satisfaction of charge (Section 82, Form CHG-4). Add it to your process.
Creating a charge may also need member approval, for example a special resolution under Section 180(1)(a) when mortgaging the whole undertaking. Check this.

title: Appointing a statutory auditor
law: Sections 139, 141, 173 and 177, Companies Act, 2013; Companies (Audit and Auditors) Rules, 2014
summary: Covers the first auditor after incorporation, appointment at the first AGM and the special rules for government companies.
when: After incorporation, when the first auditor must be named, and at the first AGM.
applies: All companies; separate route for government companies

steps.d: Choose an independent practising chartered accountant or firm eligible under Section 141 and write to ask for their consent.
Obtain a written consent and a certificate confirming the eligibility conditions of Section 141.
Give notice to all directors. Pass a resolution to appoint the first auditor, fix remuneration and authorise a director or company secretary to act.
steps.time: Within 30 days of incorporation; at least 7 days' notice (shorter for urgent business)

steps.d: Issue an appointment letter on the company's letterhead.

steps.t: File ADT-1 for the first auditor
steps.d: File with the Registrar.
steps.time: Within 15 days of the board meeting

steps.t: If the Board misses the 30 days
steps.d: Tell the members about the failure. Members appoint the first auditor at an EGM, which must give the Section 102 explanatory statement. The auditor holds office until the first AGM.

The CAG appoints the first auditor within 60 days. If CAG does not, the Board appoints within the next 30 days. If the Board fails, members appoint within 60 days at an EGM. The auditor holds office until the first AGM.
Give notice to directors. Where an audit committee is required under Section 177, it recommends the auditor to the Board; otherwise the Board proposes one. Approve the AGM notice.
steps.time: At least 7 days' notice (shorter for urgent business)

steps.t: Issue the AGM notice and hold the AGM
steps.d: Send notice at least 21 clear days ahead. Pass an ordinary resolution appointing the auditor to hold office until the sixth AGM.
steps.time: 21 clear days (shorter with consent of members holding 95% of paid-up capital)

steps.d: Issue the appointment letter and file ADT-1.
steps.time: Within 15 days (the reference note says of the board meeting)

steps.d: The CAG appoints an auditor each financial year; the auditor holds office until the AGM.
steps.time: Within 180 days of the start of the financial year

forms.purpose: Notice of appointment of auditor to the Registrar

checklist: Written consent from the auditor received
Board notice sent at least 7 days ahead
AGM notice sent 21 clear days ahead

meetings.title: Board meeting to appoint the first auditor
meetings.notice_days: At least 7 days (shorter for urgent business)

meetings.title: EGM to appoint first auditor if Board failed
meetings.notice_days: At least 21 clear days (shorter with consent)

meetings.title: Board meeting to propose auditor and call first AGM
meetings.notice_days: At least 7 days (shorter for urgent business)

resolutions.title: Appointment of first auditor by the Board
resolutions.text: RESOLVED THAT, pursuant to Section 139(6) of the Companies Act, 2013 and the Companies (Audit and Auditors) Rules, 2014, [name of auditor / firm], Chartered Accountants (Firm Registration No. [number]), having given their written consent and eligibility certificate under Section 141, be appointed first statutory auditor of {co} to hold office until the conclusion of the first Annual General Meeting, at a remuneration of Rs. [amount] plus taxes and out-of-pocket expenses. RESOLVED FURTHER THAT [name of director / company secretary] be authorised to issue the appointment letter and file Form ADT-1.

resolutions.title: Appointment of first auditor by members at an EGM
resolutions.text: RESOLVED THAT, pursuant to Section 139(6) of the Companies Act, 2013, [name of auditor / firm], Chartered Accountants (Firm Registration No. [number]), be appointed first statutory auditor of {co} to hold office until the conclusion of the first Annual General Meeting, at a remuneration of Rs. [amount] plus taxes and out-of-pocket expenses, as fixed by the Board.
resolutions.explanatory: The Board did not appoint the first auditor within 30 days of incorporation. Under Section 139(6) the members must appoint the auditor within 90 days. [Name of auditor / firm] have given written consent and certified they meet Section 141. No director is interested in this resolution.

resolutions.title: Board recommendation of auditor and approval of AGM notice
resolutions.text: RESOLVED THAT, on the recommendation of the Audit Committee [if applicable] and under Section 139(1) of the Companies Act, 2013, the appointment of [name of auditor / firm], Chartered Accountants (Firm Registration No. [number]), as statutory auditor to hold office from the conclusion of the first Annual General Meeting until the conclusion of the sixth Annual General Meeting be recommended to the members, at a remuneration of Rs. [amount]. RESOLVED FURTHER THAT the notice of the first AGM to be held on [date] be approved.

resolutions.title: Appointment of auditor at the first AGM
resolutions.text: RESOLVED THAT, pursuant to Section 139(1) of the Companies Act, 2013 and the Companies (Audit and Auditors) Rules, 2014, [name of auditor / firm], Chartered Accountants (Firm Registration No. [number]), be appointed statutory auditor of {co} to hold office from the conclusion of this meeting until the conclusion of the sixth Annual General Meeting, at a remuneration of Rs. [amount] plus taxes and out-of-pocket expenses.
resolutions.explanatory: [Name of auditor / firm] have given written consent and a certificate that they meet Section 141. Details of the auditor and the basis of the proposed remuneration are as follows: [details].

docs.title: Letter seeking consent of the auditor
paras: To [name of auditor / firm], [address].
Subject: Proposed appointment as statutory auditor of {co}.

The Board proposes to appoint you as statutory auditor of {co} under Section 139 of the Companies Act, 2013. Please send your written consent and a certificate that you meet the conditions of Section 141 and are not disqualified, along with the Peer Review details if applicable.
For {co}, [name], [designation], [date].

docs.title: Appointment letter to the auditor
paras: To [name of auditor / firm], [address].
Subject: Appointment as statutory auditor.

We inform you that you were appointed statutory auditor of {co} by [board resolution / resolution of members] dated [date], to hold office until the conclusion of [first / sixth] Annual General Meeting, at a remuneration of Rs. [amount]. Please confirm acceptance.
For {co}, [name], [designation], [date].

flags: The reference note says ADT-1 is filed within 15 days of the board meeting even for the AGM appointment (Part B). For appointment by members, ADT-1 is due within 15 days of the AGM (Rule 4(2)); check.

The reference note says the AGM resolution appoints auditor until the sixth AGM; Section 139(1) says until the conclusion of the sixth AGM, with ratification no longer needed (omitted from 2018). Confirm the current text.
The reference note says the Companies (Auditor and Auditors) Rules; correct title is Companies (Audit and Auditors) Rules, 2014.
The reference note does not mention auditor rotation limits under Section 139(2) for listed and certain other companies; check if applicable.

title: Cancelling, surrendering or deactivating a DIN
law: Section 153, Companies Act, 2013; Rule 11, Companies (Appointment and Qualification of Directors) Rules, 2014
summary: Explains when a DIN can be cancelled or deactivated by the authorities, how an individual surrenders a DIN and when a DIN is deactivated automatically.
when: When a person holds two DINs, got a DIN wrongly, has died or become incapable, or has not completed KYC.

steps.t: Check the ground for cancellation or deactivation
steps.d: The Central Government (Regional Director) can cancel or deactivate a DIN on application with fee if: the DIN is a duplicate (data is merged into the valid DIN); it was obtained wrongly or by fraud; the person has died; a court has declared the person of unsound mind; or the person was declared insolvent. For fraud, the person gets a hearing first.
The individual files DIR-5 with the MCA to surrender the DIN.
docs: Proof of identity (self-attested PAN, passport etc.)
Affidavit that the retained DIN will be updated with all CIN and LLPIN associations
Death certificate (if the person has died)

steps.d: The MCA checks the form and documents. If satisfied, the Central Government may approve the surrender.
A DIN is deactivated if the holder does not file DIR-3 KYC or DIR-3 KYC web service in time under Rule 12A.
A deactivated DIN is reactivated only after filing DIR-3 KYC or the web service with the prescribed fee.

forms.purpose: Application for surrender or cancellation of DIN

checklist: Identify which DIN to keep and which to surrender
Death certificate or court order if needed
KYC status checked for deactivated DINs

docs.title: Affidavit for surrender of DIN
paras: I, [name], son/daughter of [name], aged [age], resident of [address], holding DIN [DIN to be retained] and DIN [DIN to be surrendered], state on oath as follows.
1. I am the holder of the two DINs above and wish to surrender DIN [DIN to be surrendered].
2. The DIN [DIN to be retained] will be updated with all CIN and LLPIN associations of the surrendered DIN.
3. The facts above are true and nothing has been concealed.
Deponent, [date], [place]. Verification: verified at [place] on [date] that the contents are true.

flags: The reference note names the Regional Director (Northern Region), Noida. The Central Government delegates this to the Regional Director; check the current delegation.
The reference note's grounds follow Rule 11(1); check the current Rule 11 text for any amendments.

title: Re-appointing a director who retires by rotation
law: Sections 152(6) and (7), 159, 162, 164 and 170, Companies Act, 2013; SS-1 and SS-2; Companies (Appointment and Qualification of Directors) Rules, 2014; Companies (Meetings of Board and its Powers) Rules, 2014
summary: Sets out which directors retire by rotation at the AGM and how they are re-appointed.
when: Every AGM, for directors liable to retire.
applies: Public companies (private companies only if their AOA adopt the rule)

steps.d: Unless the AOA says otherwise, at least two-thirds of the total directors must be liable to retire by rotation. The reference note excludes independent, nominee, additional, alternate and small shareholder directors from the count.

One-third of the directors liable to rotation retire at each AGM. Those longest in office since last appointment retire first. If the number is not three or a multiple of three, take the nearest whole number. For directors appointed the same day, they agree or draw lots.
Ask each retiring director whether they will accept re-appointment.
Get a declaration that the director is not disqualified under Section 164.
Send notice with agenda and draft resolutions. Approve the re-appointment and recommend it in the AGM notice. Prepare and circulate minutes.
steps.time: At least 7 clear days before the meeting

steps.d: Prepare the notice with explanatory statement and a separate ordinary resolution for each director. Send to every member at the registered address.
steps.time: At least 21 clear days before the AGM

steps.d: Members vote on each resolution. If approved, the director is re-appointed. If not approved and the meeting is adjourned, and the vacancy is still not filled at the adjourned meeting, the retiring director is deemed re-appointed unless disqualified or a re-appointment resolution was expressly rejected. Prepare and circulate minutes.
Update the register of directors and KMP and their shareholding under Section 170.
Re-appointment on retirement by rotation is not a change in office, so DIR-12 is not needed. It is needed if the director's designation changes.

forms.purpose: Particulars of directors (needed only on change of designation)

checklist: List of directors liable to retire prepared
Retiring director identified by length of service
Consent of the retiring director received
Board notice, agenda and draft resolutions sent 7 clear days ahead
AGM notice sent 21 clear days ahead
Minutes of Board and AGM prepared
Register of directors and KMP updated

resolutions.title: Board recommendation for re-appointment
resolutions.text: RESOLVED THAT, [name of director] (DIN [number]), who retires by rotation at the ensuing Annual General Meeting under Section 152(6) of the Companies Act, 2013 and being eligible, having given consent and a declaration in Form DIR-8 under Section 164, be recommended to the members for re-appointment as a director liable to retire by rotation. RESOLVED FURTHER THAT the notice of the Annual General Meeting to be held on [date] with this item be approved.

resolutions.title: Re-appointment of retiring director
resolutions.text: RESOLVED THAT, pursuant to Section 152(6) of the Companies Act, 2013, [name of director] (DIN [number]), who retires by rotation at this meeting and being eligible offers himself/herself for re-appointment, be re-appointed as a director of {co}, liable to retire by rotation.
resolutions.explanatory: Details of the director as required under SS-2 and Regulation 36 where applicable: [age, qualifications, experience, other directorships, shareholding]. The director is interested in this resolution to the extent of this re-appointment.

docs.title: Consent letter from retiring director
paras: To the Board of Directors of {co}.

I, [name], Director (DIN [number]), retire by rotation at the Annual General Meeting to be held on [date]. I am willing / not willing to be re-appointed. If willing, I confirm I am not disqualified under Section 164 and enclose my declaration in DIR-8.
[Name], [date].

flags: The reference note excludes nominee, additional, alternate and small shareholder directors from the rotation count. Section 152(6) only excludes independent directors from the total; check the AOA and the Act.
The deemed re-appointment rule in Section 152(7) has more conditions than shown (written unwillingness of the director, a lost resolution, disqualification, Section 162 limits). Check the full text.
SS-1 should be checked for the current notice rule: 7 days' notice, including a clear gap.

title: Carrying out Corporate Social Responsibility projects
law: Section 135 read with Sections 149, 198 and 381 and Schedule VII, Companies Act, 2013; Companies (CSR Policy) Rules, 2014; Rule 9, Companies (Accounts) Rules, 2014; MCA General Circular No. 14/2021 dated 25 August 2021
summary: Covers who must do CSR, the committee, policy, spending amount, unspent funds, impact assessment, accounting and reporting.
when: Every year for companies crossing the CSR thresholds in the previous financial year.
applies: Companies (including holding, subsidiary and foreign companies with an Indian branch or project office) with net worth Rs.500 crore or more, turnover Rs.1000 crore or more, or net profit Rs.5 crore or more in the preceding year

steps.d: Test the thresholds on the preceding year's net worth, turnover and net profit. Net profit leaves out profit from overseas branches and dividends from Indian companies covered by Section 135. For a foreign company, use the profit and loss account under Section 381 read with Section 198.

Set up a committee of at least 3 directors with at least 1 independent director. An unlisted public company that need not have independent directors may use 2 or more directors. No committee is needed if the CSR spend is Rs.50 lakh or less; the Board then does its work.

The Committee proposes the CSR Policy (activities from Schedule VII), the spend, an annual action plan and monitoring. It also recommends changes to the plan and the use of international organisations for design, monitoring and evaluation.
Spend at least 2% of the average net profit of the three preceding years. If the company is less than three years old, use the years available.

Give at least 7 days' notice. The Board approves the CSR Policy and the annual action plan, makes sure projects run through the company or implementing agencies under Rule 4, keeps overheads within 5% of the CSR spend, and ensures impact assessment cost stays within the cap in the reference note (see flags).
Move the unspent amount to a special 'Unspent CSR Account' in a scheduled bank. Spend it within 3 financial years. Any balance goes to a Schedule VII fund within 30 days after the third year ends.
steps.time: Transfer within 30 days of year end; 3 years to spend

steps.d: Move unspent amounts for non-ongoing projects to a Schedule VII fund as per MCA circular 14/2021, point 3.15.

Surplus from CSR projects goes back into the project, or to the Unspent CSR Account, or to a Schedule VII fund, within 6 months of year end. Excess spending may be set off against the next 3 years if the Board approves.
steps.time: 6 months for surplus; next 3 years for set-off

steps.d: If average CSR obligation is Rs.10 crore or more, an independent agency must assess each project with outlay of Rs.1 crore or more that finished at least one year ago.
The CFO or person in charge of finance certifies that the money was used for the approved purposes and in the approved way. The Board also satisfies itself on this.

Record CSR spend in the profit and loss statement: amount spent plus contractual liabilities, less any excess carried forward. Show unpaid amounts, earmarked ongoing project funds, other unspent amounts and carried-forward excess in the balance sheet as the reference note states.

Give details in the CSR annexure of the Board's report, with reasons if the full amount was not spent and any impact assessment report. Put the committee composition, policy and approved projects on the website. Report spending in Form CSR-2, part of AOC-4 on the MCA portal.

forms.purpose: Report on CSR spending (part of AOC-4 and its variants)
Filing of financial statements, with CSR-2

checklist: Thresholds tested on the preceding year's numbers
CSR Committee formed (or Board acting if spend is Rs.50 lakh or less)
CSR Policy approved by the Board
CSR amount calculated at 2% of 3-year average net profit
Unspent CSR Account opened for ongoing projects
Policy and projects on the website

meetings.title: Board meeting to form the CSR Committee
Board meeting to approve CSR Policy and annual action plan
Board meeting on year-end unspent CSR amount and set-off

resolutions.title: Constitution of CSR Committee
resolutions.text: RESOLVED THAT, under Section 135 of the Companies Act, 2013 and the Companies (Corporate Social Responsibility Policy) Rules, 2014, a CSR Committee of the Board be formed with [names of directors] as members, of whom [name] is an independent director, and [name] as Chairperson. RESOLVED FURTHER THAT the Committee formulate the CSR Policy, recommend the annual spend and action plan and monitor implementation.

resolutions.title: Approval of CSR Policy
resolutions.text: RESOLVED THAT the CSR Policy recommended by the CSR Committee, covering activities from Schedule VII of the Companies Act, 2013, be approved. RESOLVED FURTHER THAT the composition of the CSR Committee, the CSR Policy and the approved projects be placed on the website of {co}.

resolutions.title: Approval of annual action plan and CSR spend
resolutions.text: RESOLVED THAT the annual action plan for the financial year [year], as recommended by the CSR Committee, with a total CSR spend of Rs. [amount] (being 2% of the average net profit of the three preceding financial years), through [implementing agency / directly], be approved under Section 135 of the Companies Act, 2013. RESOLVED FURTHER THAT administrative overheads not exceed 5% of the CSR spend.

resolutions.title: Unspent CSR amount
resolutions.text: RESOLVED THAT the unspent CSR amount of Rs. [amount] for ongoing projects for financial year [year] be transferred to the Unspent CSR Account with [bank] within 30 days of year end, under Section 135(6) of the Companies Act, 2013. RESOLVED FURTHER THAT the unspent amount of Rs. [amount] for other than ongoing projects be transferred to [fund specified in Schedule VII] within 6 months of year end.

resolutions.title: Set-off of excess CSR spend
resolutions.text: RESOLVED THAT the excess CSR amount of Rs. [amount] spent in financial year [year] be carried forward for set-off against the CSR obligation of the next three financial years, under Rule 7 of the Companies (Corporate Social Responsibility Policy) Rules, 2014.

docs.title: CFO certificate on use of CSR funds
paras: I, [name], Chief Financial Officer of {co}, certify that the CSR amount of Rs. [amount] disbursed during the financial year [year] has been used for the purposes and in the manner approved by the Board.
[Name], [designation], [date].

flags: The reference note gives the net profit threshold as Rs.500 crore. Section 135(1) says net profit of Rs.5 crore or more. Net worth Rs.500 crore and turnover Rs.1000 crore are correct.

The reference note says impact assessment spend may be 2% of CSR spend or Rs.50 lakh, whichever is higher. Rule 4(6) says 5% of the year's CSR spend or Rs.50 lakh, whichever is higher. Check the current text.
The COVID-19 research proviso for 2020-21 to 2022-23 has expired; it has no use for later years.
The reference note's Board step says surplus must be moved within 6 months of year end; confirm against Rule 7(2) for exact wording.
The reference note says set-off may be approved by the Board for the next 3 years; confirm the Board resolution requirement in Rule 7(3).

title: Making a contribution to a political party
summary: Sets who may contribute to a political party, the board approval needed, how to pay and what to disclose.
when: When a company wants to give money, directly or indirectly, to a political party.
applies: Companies that are not government companies and have existed for at least three financial years

steps.d: Check the company is not a government company and has existed for at least three financial years.
Pass a resolution approving the contribution to the political party.
A public company files a copy of the board resolution with the Registrar. A private company need not.
Pay by account payee cheque, account payee bank draft, bank transfer through ECS, or any instrument under a lawfully notified scheme for political contributions.
Show the total amount contributed in the profit and loss account for the year.

forms.purpose: Filing of board resolution (public companies only)

checklist: Company is at least three financial years old
Board resolution passed at a meeting
Payment by approved banking channel only
Amount shown in profit and loss account

meetings.title: Board meeting to approve the political contribution

resolutions.title: Approval of political contribution
resolutions.text: RESOLVED THAT, under Section 182 of the Companies Act, 2013, a contribution of Rs. [amount in Rs.] be made to [name of political party] during the financial year [year], by [account payee cheque / bank draft / electronic transfer / notified instrument]. RESOLVED FURTHER THAT [name of director / company secretary] be authorised to make the payment and to file Form MGT-14 and any other documents needed.

flags: The reference note does not mention the cap on contributions. Section 182 as I know it limits contributions to 7.5% of the average net profit of the three preceding years; the 2017 amendment removing the cap was struck down by the Supreme Court in 2024. Verify the current position.
The reference note asks only for the total amount to be disclosed. Section 182(3) as restored needs the amount and the party-wise details; verify.

The reference note requires MGT-14 only for public companies and a resolution at a Board meeting; the Board meetings rules list political contributions among powers to be exercised at a meeting. Confirm whether MGT-14 is required for your case.

title: Striking a company's name off the register
law: Section 248, Companies Act, 2013 read with Rule 24, Companies (Management and Administration) Rules, 2014 and the Companies (Removal of Names of Companies from the Register of Companies) Rules, 2016
summary: Lets a company that has stopped business ask the Registrar to remove its name, after clearing its dues and getting member approval.
when: When a company is no longer carrying on business and wants to close down.
applies: All companies, including private companies; certain categories cannot be struck off

steps.d: The reference note lists grounds: the company did not start business within one year of incorporation; it has not carried on business for the two preceding financial years and has not applied for dormant status; the subscribers did not pay the subscription and no Section 10A declaration was filed within 180 days; or physical verification showed no business.

Approve the application, authorise a director to file it, and either get written consent of 75% of members by paid-up capital, or fix the general meeting and approve the notice with explanatory statement and authorise who issues it.

If the company is regulated (RBI, SEBI, IRDAI or another law, such as NBFCs, housing finance, insurance, market intermediaries, collective investment schemes, asset managers), get a no-objection certificate from the regulator.
Pass a special resolution for removal of the name, certified by every director. Or use written consent of 75% of members by paid-up capital on the application date.
File the special resolution with fees.

Every director gives a notarised indemnity bond in STK-3 and a notarised affidavit in STK-4. Foreign nationals and NRIs notarise, apostille or consularise as required. A wholly owned government company or its wholly owned subsidiary uses STK-3A, signed by an authorised representative not below Under Secretary rank.

steps.t: Prepare the statement of accounts and litigation statement
steps.d: Prepare assets and liabilities as in STK-8, made up to a day within 30 days before the application and certified by a chartered accountant. Prepare a statement of pending litigation if any.

File STK-2 certified by a practising CA, CS or cost accountant, with the fee of Rs.10,000, with the Registrar, C-PACE. Attach the listed documents. If a director has no DSC, attach a manually signed copy.
docs: Declaration of closure of bank accounts
CA certificate (no litigation, no liabilities, no creditors, no bank account, no business)

steps.t: Put the application on the website
steps.d: If the company has a website, display the application until it is decided.
If the Registrar finds defects, resubmit within 15 days. A second defect gives a further 15 days. Otherwise the form is treated as invalid.

The Registrar publishes notice in STK-5 or STK-6 (and STK-5A for publications under Section 248(1)): on the MCA website, in the Official Gazette, and in a leading English newspaper and a vernacular newspaper in the state of the registered office. The Registrar also informs tax and other authorities, who have 30 days to object.

After the notice period, unless the company shows cause, the Registrar may strike off the name and publish notice in the Official Gazette in STK-7. The company stands dissolved on publication. Liability of directors, officers and members continues as if the company had not been dissolved.

forms.purpose: Application to remove the company's name

forms.deadline: Made up to within 30 days before the application

checklist: Overdue financial statements and annual returns filed up to the year business stopped
Company is not in a category that cannot be struck off
Special resolution or 75% written consent in hand
STK-3 and STK-4 notarised for every director
STK-8 certified by a chartered accountant
Bank accounts closed with closure letter

meetings.title: Board meeting to approve the strike-off application
EGM to remove the company name
meetings.notice_days: At least 21 clear days (shorter with consent)

resolutions.title: Approval of the strike-off application
resolutions.text: RESOLVED THAT, under Section 248 of the Companies Act, 2013, the company apply to the Registrar, C-PACE, for removal of its name from the register, as it is not carrying on any business. RESOLVED FURTHER THAT an Extraordinary General Meeting be held on [date] at [time] at [place] and the draft notice with the explanatory statement be approved, and [name of director / officer] be authorised to issue it. RESOLVED FURTHER THAT [name of director] be authorised to file Form STK-2 with the documents and fee and to file Form MGT-14.

resolutions.title: Special resolution for removal of the company's name
resolutions.text: RESOLVED THAT, under Section 248(2) of the Companies Act, 2013 and the Companies (Removal of Names of Companies from the Register of Companies) Rules, 2016, an application be made to the Registrar for removal of the name of {co} from the register of companies. RESOLVED FURTHER THAT [name of director] be authorised to sign and file Form STK-2 and other documents and to appear before the Registrar.
resolutions.explanatory: The company has not carried on any business since [date] and has paid or settled all its liabilities. The company seeks removal of its name under Section 248(2). The directors have given indemnity bonds and affidavits. No director or member is interested except as a member.

docs.title: Written consent of members for strike off
paras: I/We, [name of member], holder(s) of [number] shares of {co} (paid-up value Rs. [amount]), consent to the application to the Registrar for removal of the name of {co} from the register of companies under Section 248(2) of the Companies Act, 2013.
[Name], [folio number], [date]. (The consenting members together must hold at least 75% of the paid-up share capital on the date of the application.)

docs.title: Declaration for closure of bank accounts
paras: We, the directors of {co}, declare that all bank accounts of the company have been closed as of [date] and no bank account is operating.
[Names and DINs of directors], [date].

docs.title: Letter waiving liabilities
paras: To the Registrar of Companies, C-PACE.
{co} states that all liabilities, if any, owed by it to [name] stand waived as of [date]. No statutory or non-statutory liability and no sundry creditor remains.
For {co}, [name], [designation], [date].

docs.title: Declaration and undertaking for PAN and TAN surrender
paras: {co} undertakes to surrender its PAN [PAN] and TAN [TAN] on strike off and to settle any tax dues.
For {co}, [name], [designation], [date].

flags: The reference note step 1 mixes up the grounds on which the Registrar may act under Section 248(1) with the company's own application under Section 248(2). A company can apply on its own after extinguishing its liabilities; check the Act.

The rules bar an application if within the last three months the company changed its name or registered office, disposed of property or rights, or has a pending Tribunal application. The reference note does not say this; check Rule 4.
The reference note asks for STK-3 indemnity bond, STK-4 affidavit and STK-8 statement; verify the form list and fee of Rs.10,000 on the MCA portal.
The reference note text for step 2 lists the written consent route and the general meeting route both under the Board agenda; you need only one of them.
The reference note numbering of the notices (STK-5, STK-5A, STK-6) is hard to follow in the original; confirm which applies to the application under Section 248(2).

title: Compounding an offence under the Companies Act
law: Section 441, Companies Act, 2013; Companies (Adjudication of Penalties) Rules, 2014 as named in the reference note; MCA circulars; Section 134(3)(q) read with Rule 8(5)(v), Companies (Accounts) Rules, 2014
summary: Lets a company settle certain offences by paying a compounding fee, to avoid prosecution.
when: When the company or its officers have committed a compoundable default and want to settle it.
applies: All companies; the authority depends on the fine, Regional Director up to Rs.25 lakh and NCLT above

steps.t: Check if the offence can be compounded
steps.d: Offences punishable with fine only, with fine or imprisonment, or with fine or imprisonment or both can be compounded. Offences punishable with imprisonment only, or with imprisonment and fine, cannot.
If the fine is up to Rs.25 lakh, apply to the Regional Director. If it is above Rs.25 lakh, apply to the NCLT having jurisdiction.
Take note of the offence, approve filing the application, and authorise a director or company secretary to sign it and appear.
Describe the company, the nature and date of the offence, the reasons, whether the default is corrected, and ask for compounding with an assurance of future compliance.
docs: Affidavit and undertaking by authorised signatory

steps.d: File through GNL-1 on the MCA portal, addressed to the RD through the jurisdictional Registrar, and pay the fees.
File a physical petition in Form NCLT-1 with documents and fees (demand draft or court fee stamps). Serve copies on the Registrar and others if needed.
The Registrar sends a report to the RD or NCLT on the background, whether the default is corrected and whether compounding is recommended.
The authority may issue notice and fix a hearing. The company's authorised representative appears and may be asked for more documents.
The authority passes an order stating the fee and any directions. Pay the fee in the time stated, usually by MCA challan or demand draft, and send proof to the authority and the Registrar.

steps.t: File the order with the Registrar
steps.d: File the order in INC-28. Delay can attract further penalty.

If no prosecution has started, none can start afterwards. If it is pending, the Registrar asks the court to withdraw it. Future breaches of the same kind remain punishable. Disclose compounding in the Board's report.
steps.time: In the Board's report for the year

checklist: Authority identified from the fine amount
Application drafted with reasons and rectification
Compounding fee paid and proof sent

meetings.title: Board meeting to approve compounding application

resolutions.title: Approval of the compounding application
resolutions.text: RESOLVED THAT the Board takes note of the default under Section [section] of the Companies Act, 2013 relating to [description of default], occurring on [date]. RESOLVED FURTHER THAT the company apply for compounding of the offence under Section 441 to the [Regional Director / National Company Law Tribunal, bench at place]. RESOLVED FURTHER THAT [name of director / company secretary] be authorised to sign and file the application and to appear before the authority.

docs.title: Application for compounding of offence
paras: Before the [Regional Director, region / National Company Law Tribunal, bench]. In the matter of {co}, [CIN], registered office at [address]. Application under Section 441 of the Companies Act, 2013.
1. The company was incorporated on [date] and carries on [business].
2. The company or its officers committed a default under Section [section] on [date], being [nature of default].
3. The default occurred because [reasons]. The default has / has not been corrected on [date] by [action].
4. The company prays that the offence be compounded and gives its assurance to comply with the law in future.
For {co}, [name], [designation], [date].

flags: The reference note cites the Adjudication of Penalties Rules, which deal with Section 454. Compounding is governed by Section 441 and its own rules; check the correct rule set.

The reference note omits Section 441 limits: the compounding fee cannot exceed the maximum fine, and an offence cannot be compounded again if it is repeated within three years of an earlier compounding. Check Section 441.
The reference note gives INC-28 within 7 days of the order and the Board's report disclosure under Rule 8(5)(v); confirm the clause references.
The reference note says the NCLT hears cases above Rs.25 lakh; check the current wording of Section 441(1) on who may compound which offence.
